summary: Traffic-engineering link attributes were first used with RSVP-TE, but newer applications like Segment Routing Policy and Loop-Free Alternates also use them. The existing advertisements can't carry application-specific values or show which applications use them. This document defines IS-IS advertisements that can. It obsoletes RFC 8919.

eli5.summary: One road sign used to serve every vehicle type. This lets the sign show separate notes for bikes and trucks, and say who each note is for.

subtitle: How IS-IS tells routers which applications may use a link attribute, and lets each application have its own value.

tldr.problem: IS-IS link attributes were built for RSVP-TE, but Segment Routing Policy and Loop-Free Alternates use them too. Routers could not tell which application an advertisement was for, or give each application its own value for the same link.
tldr.mechanism: A new Application-Specific Link Attributes sub-TLV (type 16) and a new Application-Specific SRLG TLV (type 238) carry an application bit mask next to the attribute values, so each advertisement names the applications that must use it.
tldr.outcome: Applications can share or separate link attributes cleanly, and new applications can be added without changing the format. This document obsoletes RFC 8919 and clarifies how zero-length bit masks work.

facts.label: Bit mask length
facts.value: 0 to 8 octets each for SABM and UDABM

today: RFC 9479 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2023. It obsoletes RFC 8919 and has not itself been obsoleted. The matching OSPF specification is RFC 9492.

sections.title: The Ambiguity Problem
sections.content:
IS-IS has advertised traffic-engineering link attributes since RFC 5305, with later additions in RFC 5307, RFC 6119, RFC 7308 and RFC 8570. These were tied to MPLS traffic engineering with RSVP, called RSVP-TE (RFC 3209).

Newer applications, such as Segment Routing (SR) Policy (RFC 9256) and Loop-Free Alternates (RFC 5286), want many of the same attributes. That creates two problems. First, if RSVP-TE runs on only some links, a router acting as an RSVP-TE head end sees an attribute advertised for another application and assumes RSVP-TE is enabled on that link. Its path setup then fails. Second, the old advertisements cannot carry a different value for each application on the same link.

The RFC defines an application as a technology that uses link attribute advertisements, and sets three needs: say which applications use an advertisement, allow per-application values, and avoid duplicating a link and attribute pair when one value can be shared.
sections.eli5: Imagine a school notice board where every note is read by both the bus drivers and the cafeteria. A note meant for the cafeteria confuses the drivers. This RFC adds a label saying who each note is for.

sections.title: Legacy Advertisements
sections.content:
Before this RFC, the attributes lived in sub-TLVs of the TLVs that advertise neighbor information. Examples are type 3 (administrative group), 9 (maximum link bandwidth), 10 (maximum reservable link bandwidth), 11 (unreserved bandwidth), 14 (extended administrative group), 18 (TE default metric) and types 33 to 39 for delay, loss and bandwidth metrics.

Shared Risk Link Group (SRLG) information used two TLVs: TLV 138 for links identified by IPv4 addresses and unnumbered links, and TLV 139 for IPv6. RFC 6119 prohibits TLV 139 when TLV 138 can be used.

The RFC calls these the legacy advertisements. They carry no information about which application they are for.
sections.eli5: The old notes had no "for" line at all. Everyone had to guess whether a note was meant for them.

sections.title: The Application Identifier Bit Mask
sections.content:
Every new advertisement starts with an application identifier bit mask. It is really two masks. The SABM covers standard applications, whose bits are assigned in an IANA registry. The UDABM covers user-defined applications, whose bits are not managed by IANA or any other standards body.

The encoding is two length octets, then the SABM, then the UDABM. Each mask is 0 to 8 octets long, and the length SHOULD be the minimum needed to send all the bits that are set. The first length octet also carries the L-flag (legacy flag). Standard bits are sent starting at bit 0, and three are defined: R-bit for RSVP-TE, S-bit for SR Policy and F-bit for LFA (all LFA types).

Undefined bits that are sent MUST be sent as 0 and ignored on receipt. Bits that are not sent are treated as 0. Bits an implementation does not support MUST be ignored.
sections.eli5: It is a row of little switches, one for each kind of user. Flip the switch for a user and the note is for them. Unflipped switches mean it is not.

sections.title: The ASLA Sub-TLV and Application-Specific SRLG TLV
sections.content:
The Application-Specific Link Attributes sub-TLV has type 16. It holds the bit mask, then link attribute sub-sub-TLVs whose formats match the existing ones from RFC 5305, RFC 7308 and RFC 8570. The sub-sub-TLV type reuses the legacy sub-TLV number. If either mask length is greater than 8, the whole sub-TLV MUST be ignored.

With the L-flag clear and a non-zero mask length, every application in the mask MUST use the attributes in this sub-TLV. With the L-flag set, those applications MUST use the legacy advertisements instead, and any sub-sub-TLVs in the sub-TLV MUST be ignored. The L-flag must match across all sub-TLVs for a link, or it is treated as set. The net result is that an application uses either ASLA values or legacy values, never both.

Several sub-TLVs for one link are allowed. If they conflict for the same application, attribute and link, the first one in the lowest-numbered LSP MUST be used.

SRLGs use a separate Application-Specific SRLG TLV, type 238. It holds the neighbor System-ID and pseudonode ID (7 octets), the bit mask, link identifier sub-TLVs and 4-octet SRLG values. One TLV covers IPv4, IPv6 and unnumbered links. At least one set of link identifiers MUST be present.
sections.eli5: Each note now has a "for" line (the switches) and the actual message. If the "for" line says "use the old notice board", readers go look there instead.

sections.title: Special Cases and Zero-Length Masks
sections.content:
Some attributes need extra rules. Maximum link bandwidth belongs to the link, not an application, so different values for one link MUST NOT be advertised, and if they are, all values MUST be ignored. Maximum reservable bandwidth and unreserved bandwidth are RSVP-TE specific, so only the R-bit may be set. Advertisements with other bits set MUST be ignored.

The RFC also allows zero-length masks for both SABM and UDABM. Such an advertisement is for any application, but it MUST be used only when no advertisement with a non-zero mask and a matching bit exists for the link. Otherwise it MUST NOT be used. If a new application is later introduced and that is not wanted, existing advertisements MUST be readvertised with an explicit set of applications first.
sections.eli5: Some notes, like how wide the road is, are true for everybody, so only one version may exist. A note with no "for" line means "everyone, unless a more specific note exists".

sections.title: Enablement and Migration
sections.content:
Whether an advertisement shows that an application is enabled on a link depends on the application. For RSVP-TE, ASLAs imply RSVP is enabled on the link. For SR Policy, they do not: SR Policy is implicitly enabled on all links in the SR-enabled topology, and the attributes only support path constraints. For LFA, enablement is by local configuration.

The standard applications may keep using legacy advertisements if the application is RSVP-TE, or if it is SR Policy or LFA and either RSVP-TE is not deployed anywhere or its links and values are fully congruent. New applications MUST NOT use legacy advertisements.

As long as any legacy router has one of these applications enabled, all routers MUST use only legacy advertisements, and ASLAs for them MUST NOT be sent. After all routers are upgraded, the steps are: send ASLAs alongside legacy ones while receivers keep using legacy, enable ASLA use everywhere, then remove the legacy advertisements. Only then can values differ per application on a link.
sections.eli5: If some people still read only the old board, you keep posting there. Once everybody can read the new board, you move over and take down the old one.

sections.title: Security and Changes from RFC 8919
sections.content:
IS-IS security is covered by ISO 10589, RFC 5304 and RFC 5310. Where attackers might reach the routing domain, the stronger authentication mechanisms SHOULD be used. Tampering with these advertisements can affect the applications that use them, including TE, but since each advertisement is limited to specific applications, so is the impact.

This document replaces RFC 8919. The LSR working group found confusion about zero-length masks, because the old text said such advertisements were "permitted", which suggested they were optional. The sections on the sub-TLV, the SRLG TLV and zero-length masks were changed to say exactly when they MUST and MUST NOT be used.
sections.eli5: The old rule said a no-"for" note was "allowed", and people read that as "optional". The new rule says exactly when it counts and when it does not.

fields.desc: Reserved. SHOULD be sent as 0 and MUST be ignored.
